newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-VW Q1 sales rise but Germany lags.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-VW Q1 sales rise but Germany lags.

text.p: German carmaker Volkswagen AG said on Monday its first quarter net profit rose nearly 50 percent and sales increased 10 percent -- mainly abroad due to a slowdown in the German market and with help from the dollar.
Net profit for the first three months of 1997 rose 48 percent to 172 million marks ($99.6 million) from 116 million marks in the 1996 quarter as sales rose 10 percent to 24.47 billion marks.

The carmaker said its results were hurt by a Spanish truck drivers' strike in February which halted production and noted the contribution of parent company Volkswagen, which reported a 36 percent rise in net profit to 122 million marks.
The strong start to 1997, which follows record net profit of 678 million marks in 1996, prompted the usually conservative carmaker to reaffirm it would post higher results for the year.
"Provided that economic conditions and also the demand for automobiles remain steady, we expect better results in 1997 at both the parent and group levels," VW said in a statement.
VW shares surged on the results, ending bourse trade up 41 marks at 1,198 marks and outpacing a two percent rise in Germany's blue-chip DAX index to 3,528.78 points.

The Wolfsburg-based carmaker said global customer deliveries rose 9.6 percent to 1.034 million vehicles, including a nine percent rise in U.S. sales to 29,526 vehicles -- its best results in the United States in seven years.
But VW's German deliveries fell five percent to 235,954 vehicles, outpacing the German vehicle industry's four percent drop in domestic production to 1.24 million vehicles.
"German carmakers in general experienced dampened demand at the start of 1997," VW said in a statement.

VW noted that vehicle imports to Germany grew three percent during the quarter to 757,000 vehicles but said it still remained the top seller even though its German market share fell to 27.1 percent from 27.3 percent last year.
Many Asian carmakers, particularly from South Korea, have been offering massive rebates to attract buyers but they have not generally been matched by major European rivals.

Despite the weak German sales, VW kept up its international expansion and reported a 15 percent rise in foreign deliveries to 799,831 vehicles and a nine percent gain in foreign production to 638,678 vehicles.

Its two foreign brands, Spanish-based Seat and Skoda of the Czech Republic, both reported increases in customer deliveries. Skoda sales surged 21 percent to 68,049 and Seat's rose eight percent to 93,876.

VW's luxury carmaker, Audi AG, reported a 19 percent rise in customer deliveries to 137,129 vehicles while Volkswagen's deliveries were up 7.4 percent to 734,731, making up the vast of the group's deliveries of 1.033 million vehicles, which was up 9.6 percent over the 1996 quarter.
Audi's sales were particularly strong in the United States which rose 34 percent to 7,716 units in a continued recovery from the early 1990s collapse due to allegations of malfunctioning cars.
VW also said west European sales outside Germany rose 7.7 percent to 373,747 units despite the region's new vehicle registrations falling 1.3 percent in the quarter.

Among other regions of the world, VW said its sales in Brazil remained strong, rising 21 percent to 159,350 units. Customer deliveries in all of Latin America and Africa rose about 18 percent to 197,567 vehicles.
In China, VW sales rose 29 percent to 67,269 vehicles and outpaced the country's 25 percent growth rate in new vehicle sales during the three-month period.
